Summary:

  • Japan’s economy shrank an annualised 0.1% in Q3, but BOJ hawk Takata argued for nimble hikes. The yen and JGBs barely moved.
  • China’s industrial output, retail sales and investment all missed forecasts. Home prices fell for a 41st month.
  • Korean chipmakers led regional losses, with SK Hynix down more than 6%, following weekend Nvidia and export-curb headlines.
  • US futures gave up early gains ahead of Fed Chair Warsh’s speech at 17:00 GMT and Nvidia results on Tuesday.
  • Brent held near $95 despite unconfirmed Iranian claims about a tanker sinking. Gold eased to around $3,873 and silver fell more than 3%.
  • China confirmed a Xi-Trump-Putin summit in Shenzhen on November 19.

Asian markets slipped on Monday as soft data from Japan and China met hawkish messages from central banks. Chipmakers led the losses as worries mounted over AI demand and US export curbs ahead of Nvidia’s results.

Japan Japan’s economy contracted an annualised 0.1% in the third quarter, its first decline in four quarters and short of forecasts for 0.3% growth. Consumption fell as inflation squeezed households and net trade cut growth, though business investment rose a stronger-than-expected 1.6%. Economists said the miss is unlikely to derail Bank of Japan tightening. Board member Hajime Takata backed that view in a speech. He argued that 2026 marks a regime change calling for nimble, data-dependent rate hikes, and that Japan’s neutral rate may prove higher than markets expect. Markets largely shrugged off his remarks. USD/JPY was little changed around 159.65 and the 10-year JGB yield edged up to about 2.88%. The Nikkei fell about 1.6% to around 60,180 and the Topix lost roughly 0.7%.

China China’s October activity data disappointed across the board. Industrial output grew 4.8%, below the 5.3% forecast. Retail sales rose just 0.4%, and fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first ten months. New home prices fell for a 41st straight month, though the annual decline eased to its slowest in almost a year. Economists see little chance of fresh stimulus before year-end. The Shanghai Composite eased about 0.4%, while the Hang Seng bucked the trend, rising around 0.8%.

Chips and AI Korean chipmakers took the brunt of the selling. SK Hynix sank more than 6% and Samsung Electronics fell about 4%, pulling the Kospi down roughly 2.6% and the Kosdaq more than 3%. The selling followed weekend headlines on Nvidia. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shakeup” at the company, and The Wall Street Journal reported that Washington is drafting rules to curb advanced chip exports to Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore. Separately, Chinese AI developer DeepSeek reportedly began rationing its free service, citing insufficient computing power. Morgan Stanley took the other side, moving to a maximum overweight on global equities on the view that the AI investment cycle remains intact. Nvidia reports on Tuesday.

Fed and US US stock futures gave up early gains, with S&P 500 futures down about 0.2% and Nasdaq 100 futures off roughly 0.5%. Recent remarks from Fed officials Jeff Schmid, Susan Collins and Philip Jefferson all put inflation at the centre of policy, keeping a December rate hike firmly priced. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh opens a Fed conference on AI and productivity at 17:00 GMT (12:00 pm ET).

Commodities and crypto Brent was steady near $95.40 and WTI was around $87.10. Expectations of a supply surplus offset unconfirmed Iranian claims that a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. Goldman Sachs forecast Brent easing to $78 by end-2027, while flagging near-term upside risks from attacks on shipping. Gold eased to around $3,873 an ounce after Goldman cut its end-2027 forecast to $4,650, and silver fell more than 3%. Bitcoin hovered near $65,100 after hitting a four-month low around $62,000 over the weekend.

Geopolitics China confirmed that President Xi Jinping will host the first trilateral summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on November 19, alongside the APEC gathering. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

The sentiment model is neutral, but the market narrative is negative for BA given the contrast between SpaceX’s rapid innovation and Boeing’s slower pace despite larger government funding. A short position lets us profit from any near‑term price weakness while the story unfolds, and we avoid the broader defense sector where Lockheed may be insulated by other contracts. We choose the equity itself rather than an option to keep the trade simple for a swing horizon.
rationale: Musk’s tweet creates a negative perception for Boeing’s space business
Starliner still not operational, widening the performance gap with SpaceX
Short‑term market tends to punish companies highlighted in high‑visibility criticism
analysis.risk: If Boeing announces a breakthrough on Starliner or secures a major defense contract, the negative sentiment could evaporate and the stock may rebound.

Goldman’s own bullish outlook boosts investor confidence

items.title: Home Depot vs. Walmart: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
items.summary: Home Depot's Pro contractor push and Walmart's grocery-driven traffic offer two very different routes to steady growth, and their valuations diverge sharply.

analysis.summary: The article compares Home Depot and Walmart, highlighting Walmart’s larger scale but weaker short‑term liquidity and higher exposure to discretionary spending slowdowns, while noting Home Depot’s strong pro‑customer focus and solid cash flow.
analysis.catalyst: Walmart’s deteriorating current ratio and higher sensitivity to consumer budget constraints signal near‑term earnings pressure
analysis.horizon: 4-6 weeks, until Walmart’s next quarterly earnings release (Q3 FY2026) where the liquidity metrics and sales mix are confirmed
analysis.explanation: Walmart’s current ratio of about 0.8 indicates short‑term liabilities exceed assets, a red flag for a retailer that must fund inventory and store operations. Combined with a modest debt‑to‑equity of 0.7, the balance sheet looks tighter than Home Depot’s, which enjoys a 1.1 current ratio and stronger cash flow from its pro‑customer segment. As interest rates stay elevated, consumers are likely to trim discretionary spend, hitting Walmart’s non‑grocery sales harder than Home Depot’s renovation‑driven revenue. The negative sentiment from the FinBERT model reinforces the view that the market perceives these pressures as downside risk. A short position in Walmart lets us capture potential price weakness if earnings miss or if the liquidity issue forces the company to tighten credit terms.
rationale: Current ratio below 1 signals liquidity strain
Higher exposure to discretionary spend amid high rates
Negative sentiment aligns with downside risk
analysis.risk: If Walmart’s grocery sales accelerate or it announces a major cost‑cutting initiative, the stock could rally, erasing the short thesis
